boundary_rationale: The row opens at web:Ps.109.6 where an unmarked singular “him” replaces the plural accusers of the preceding row—הַפְקֵ֣ד עָלָ֣יו רָשָׁ֑ע (web:Ps.109.6 = oshb:Ps.109.6, “Set a wicked man over him”)—and no reported-speech verb (a 'saying' or 'who say' construction) introduces the shift; on the frame bytes this reads as the psalmist continuing his own prayer against a singular, representative adversary rather than resuming a quotation of the accusers’ own words. A jussive curse-chain runs unbroken through the span, opening יִֽהְיֽוּ (oshb:Ps.109.8) and carrying an interior fatherless-root echo: בָנָ֥יו יְתוֹמִ֑ים (web:Ps.109.9 = oshb:Ps.109.9, “his children be fatherless”) and, echoing it, ח֝וֹנֵ֗ן לִיתוֹמָֽיו (web:Ps.109.12 = oshb:Ps.109.12, “no one to extend kindness...to have pity on his fatherless children”)—two distinct fatherless-root spellings, swept separately: 109:9's spelling recurs in 3 verses book-wide (2 outside this span); 109:12's spelling is unique to 109:12 book-wide (1 verse), inside this span. The unit closes on יְהִֽי אַחֲרִית֥וֹ לְהַכְרִ֑ית (web:Ps.109.13 = oshb:Ps.109.13, “Let his posterity be cut off”).

A shared remembrance-root binds oshb:Ps.109.14-Ps.109.16: the verb opening יִזָּכֵ֤ר עֲוֺ֣ן אֲ֭בֹתָיו recurs as the noun זִכְרָֽם (web:Ps.109.15 = oshb:Ps.109.15, “their memory”) and again in the motive clause יַ֗עַן אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹ֥א זָכַר֮ (web:Ps.109.16 = oshb:Ps.109.16, “because he didn’t remember”). strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at v16 (doubled right-hand refrain alone) would cut the acclamation off from the survival declaration it grounds: the 1cs forms of oshb:Ps.118.17 (אָמ֥וּת, אֶֽחְיֶ֑ה, וַ֝אֲסַפֵּ֗ר) are absent from oshb:Ps.118.15-Ps.118.16, so v17 answers in the speaker's own voice what this candidate reads as vv15-16's communal acclamation.

boundary_rationale: From web:Ps.127.3 the psalm turns to a new figure, “Behold, children are a heritage of Yahweh. The fruit of the womb is his reward.”, continuing the same gift-language through the warrior's-arrows simile of web:Ps.127.4 and closing with a beatitude, “Happy is the man who has his quiver full of them. They won't be disappointed when they speak with their enemies in the gate.” (web:Ps.127.5). The seam itself turns on an addressee shift: the second-person address לָכֶ֨ם (oshb:Ps.127.2) gives way to the presentative הִנֵּ֤ה with third-person description at oshb:Ps.127.3, and nothing in these three verses returns to the house-building or city-watching figures of web:Ps.127.1-web:Ps.127.2; the heritage/reward pairing of web:Ps.127.3 is this panel's own opening claim, parallel in form to the house-and-city panel's futility claims but distinct in subject, so the two panels are kept as separate rows under the one psalm.

boundary_rationale: “עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֑ב” (oshb:Ps.135.15) -- “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.” (web:Ps.135.15) -- opens an idol polemic that runs through mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see (web:Ps.135.16), ears that cannot hear (web:Ps.135.17), to the closing verdict, “Those who make them will be like them, yes, everyone who trusts in them.” (web:Ps.135.18). This four-verse unit shows cross-psalm texture with Ps 115's idol polemic (115:4-115:8): a word-by-word byte comparison of both psalms' own text (verse_map_oshb.json) finds oshb:Ps.135.16 matching oshb:Ps.115.5 and oshb:Ps.135.18 matching oshb:Ps.115.8 letter-for-letter, while 135:15's construct chain with the article (עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם) differs from 115:4's suffixed plural (oshb:Ps.115.4: עֲֽ֭צַבֵּיהֶם), and אָזְנַ֣יִם לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ אַ֝֗ף אֵין יֶשׁ ר֥וּחַ בְּפִיהֶֽם (oshb:Ps.135.17) as a whole verse runs longer than 115:6 alone on all 3 measures taken (9 vs 8 skeleton words, 32 vs 30 consonants, 70 vs 67 codepoints), shorter only against 115:6-115:7 combined (17 skeleton words / 70 consonants / 156 codepoints with one joining space), and its clause shared with 115:6, אָזְנַ֣יִם לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ, substitutes a different verb root (יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ for oshb:Ps.115.6's יִשְׁמָ֑עוּ) inside the four-word clause the two verses set in the same slot, of which they share the first three words at byte tier. It is discussed here as a recognizable, recurring cross-psalm texture, not merged with Ps 115's own rows.

boundary_rationale: The incense-prayer opens “Yahweh, I have called on you. Come to me quickly! Listen to my voice” (web:Ps.141.1) and the simile “Let my prayer be set before you like incense” (web:Ps.141.2), Hebrew תְּפִלָּתִ֣י קְטֹ֣רֶת (oshb:Ps.141.2) -- before the guard-my-mouth petition, “Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips” (web:Ps.141.3), and the request not to be drawn into the wicked’s company (web:Ps.141.4). The four verses continue one imperative, second-person address to Yahweh—יְהוָ֣ה קְ֭רָאתִיךָ ח֣וּשָׁה (oshb:Ps.141.1), לְפָנֶ֑יךָ (oshb:Ps.141.2), יְ֭הוָה שָׁמְרָ֣ה לְפִ֑י (oshb:Ps.141.3), אַל תַּט (oshb:Ps.141.4)—closing where that address drops: no second-person form stands in any token of oshb:Ps.141.5-Ps.141.7. web:Ps.141.5 turns instead to a descriptive register that continues the same 3mp referent web:Ps.141.4 itself names (‘the workers of iniquity’ and their delicacies) through web:Ps.141.5-6.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at web:Ps.141.2's incense simile was considered, but the imperative, second-person petitions of vv3-4 continue the same opening address to Yahweh without a topic change until web:Ps.141.5, where that address drops and the register turns from petition to descriptive report—a turn that continues rather than breaks the 3mp referent web:Ps.141.4 itself names.
